# CLI and config reference

<!-- Generated by crates/cli/tests/reference_docs.rs. Do not edit by hand.
Regenerate with: UPDATE_REFERENCE=1 cargo test -p playbook --test reference_docs -->

This page lists every `playbook` command, flag and config key. It is generated from the
clap definitions and the config key table, and a test fails when it is out of date.
For what each key means and when to change it, read the [config keys page](config-keys.md).
For one line per command and who may run it, run `playbook commands`.

## Commands

### `playbook`

Configure and support Claude Code from the command line.

playbook installs hooks and a session launcher, shows the Agent Budget Dashboard, and helps with PRs, reviews, worktrees and session handoffs.

Subcommands: `adr`, `agents`, `atlassian`, `cc`, `ccd`, `ci`, `code`, `commands`, `commit`, `completions`, `config`, `deliver`, `deps`, `doc`, `doctor`, `effort`, `eval`, `gate`, `gc`, `glossary`, `handoff`, `hooks`, `learn`, `manifest`, `memory`, `migrate`, `mode`, `path`, `plan`, `plans`, `plugin`, `pr`, `prose`, `review`, `route`, `run-context`, `sanitize`, `segment`, `sessions`, `settings`, `setup`, `skills`, `state`, `statusline`, `tools`, `trust`, `uninstall`, `upgrade`, `usage`, `version`, `watch`, `worktree`

### `playbook adr`

Work with ADRs, such as the next free record number

Subcommands: `next`

### `playbook adr next`

Print the next ADR number and today's date

Creates `docs/adr` in the repo if it is missing. Prints `Next number: NNNN   Date: YYYY-MM-DD`.

### `playbook agents`

Check that agent definition files follow the playbook rules

Subcommands: `check`

### `playbook agents check`

Check every agent definition follows the agent rules

Exits 0 when all pass and 1 otherwise.

- `<AGENTS_DIR>`: Directory of agent definitions. Defaults to `plugins/playbook/agents` in the repo, else `agents` at the repo root

### `playbook atlassian`

Check the Atlassian tools the `playbook:atlassian` skill uses

Subcommands: `check`

### `playbook atlassian check`

Check the `acli` version and whether `twg` is installed

Prints one line for `acli` (`ok`, `too old` with the `brew upgrade atlassian/acli/acli` hint, `version unreadable` or `missing`) and one for `twg`. Exits 0 when `acli` is usable and 1 otherwise, so the skill can fall back to the next route. Whether the Atlassian MCP tools are connected is left to the skill.

### `playbook cc`

Start a Claude Code session, or manage sessions and worktrees

With no subcommand, starts a session with the playbook prompt and model chain. Any other arguments go to claude as they are. The subcommands do the housekeeping: list sessions, prune state, clear caches, and create worktrees. `pb` is an alias for `playbook`, so `pb cc` works too.

Example: `playbook cc --model sonnet`

- `<ARGS>`: Arguments passed through to claude

Subcommands: `bust-cache`, `clean`, `fresh`, `launch`, `list`, `prune`, `raw`, `worktree`

### `playbook cc bust-cache`

Clear caches that would freeze old settings into a session

### `playbook cc clean`

Clean up and resume a session

Clones the session named for this directory with its settings overrides stripped, then resumes the clone in `claude`, so settings, plugins and hooks reload from the current config. Starts a fresh session when none matches. The same as `playbook cc --clean`.

- `<ARGS>`: Arguments passed through to claude

### `playbook cc fresh`

Start a fresh session

Starts a new `claude` session without resuming an earlier one, with the current settings applied. The same as `playbook cc --fresh`.

- `<ARGS>`: Arguments passed through to claude

### `playbook cc launch`

Run the launcher (`playbook cc` and `playbook ccd` call it)

- `--skip-permissions`: Pass `--dangerously-skip-permissions` to claude (the `playbook ccd` form)
- `<ARGS>`: Subcommand and arguments, passed through to claude

### `playbook cc list`

List sessions for the current project

### `playbook cc prune`

Remove stale runtime state

### `playbook cc raw`

Resume a session as it was

Resumes a session in `claude` as it was, with no fork and its settings overrides kept. Starts a fresh session when none matches. The same as `playbook cc --raw`.

- `<ARGS>`: Session id to resume (default: the most recent), then arguments for claude

### `playbook cc worktree`

Create a git worktree for a branch and print its path

Prints only the path, so a shell can run `cd "$(playbook cc worktree my-branch)"`.

Example: `playbook cc worktree my-branch`

- `<BRANCH>`: Branch to create the worktree for
- `<ENV_BASE>`: Directory (relative to the repo root) holding the `.env` to copy in

### `playbook ccd`

Start a session with permission prompts skipped

The same launcher as `playbook cc`, with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` added. It replaces the old `ccd` shortcut. `pb ccd` works too.

Example: `playbook ccd fresh`

- `<ARGS>`: Subcommand and arguments, passed through to claude

### `playbook ci`

Run the repo checks that need no model (manifest, agents, settings)

Prints one line per check. Exits 0 when all pass and 1 if any fails, so it is safe in CI. A skipped check passes unless `--strict` is set.

Example: `playbook ci --strict`

- `--json`: Print one JSON object instead of text
- `--strict`: Also exit 1 when a check is skipped (for example in the wrong directory)
- `--dir <DIR>`: Run in this directory instead of the current one

### `playbook code`

Index and search the repo's source code

The index is a cache kept under the playbook state directory for this worktree. Nothing is written inside the repo.

Subcommands: `context`, `index`, `outline`, `read`, `refs`, `search`, `status`, `symbol`

### `playbook code context`

Gather the code a task needs

Describe the task in words. Finds matching declarations and text, widens text hits to the declaration around them, adds imports of the top files and tests that name a top declaration, merges overlaps and fills a size budget. Prints what did not fit.

Example: `playbook code context "add retry support to payment processing"`

- `<QUERY>`: Task, in words
- `--max-tokens <MAX_TOKENS>`: Budget in tokens for the whole text output, counted as four bytes each
- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook code index`

Build or refresh the code index for this repo

Hashes every file git lists, and reads only the ones that changed. Worktrees of one repo share one store, so content that is already stored is not parsed again. Each worktree runs once at a time.

Example: `playbook code index --json`

- `--json`: Print one JSON document
- `--rebuild`: Index everything again; a damaged store is replaced for every worktree

### `playbook code outline`

List the declarations in one file

Parses the file as it is on disk, so it works without an index and never shows old text. Prints at most 500 declarations, indented by nesting.

Example: `playbook code outline lib/payment/service.ts`

- `<PATH>`: File to outline
- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook code read`

Print numbered lines of one file

Reads the file as it is on disk. Prints at most 400 lines or 32 KiB. A range that ends past the file is cut at the end with a warning.

Example: `playbook code read lib/payment/service.ts 10:40`

- `<PATH>`: File to read
- `<LINES>`: First and last line, 1 based and inclusive, as START:END
- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook code refs`

List syntax references to a name

Finds identifiers in code that spell the name, including declarations and imports, and skips comments and strings. Every result is a candidate: nothing checks scope or types, so unrelated names that share a spelling also appear.

Example: `playbook code refs processPayment`

- `<TARGET>`: Name to look for. A dotted or scoped name uses its last part
- `--limit <LIMIT>`: Most results to show, from 1 to 200
- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook code search`

Search symbols, imports and text of this repo

Without the text flag, results are ranked in tiers: exact qualified name, exact name, name ignoring case, name prefix, import, text, then a plain substring scan. With it, only indexed text is searched. Words in the query are matched as plain text, so operators have no special meaning. Results are marked stale when a file changed after indexing.

Example: `playbook code search retry --lang python`

- `<QUERY>`: Words to look for
- `--text`: Search indexed text only
- `--path <PATH>`: Only files under this path prefix, for example `lib/payment/`
- `--lang <LANG>`: Only files of this language: rust, typescript, javascript, python or go (one of `rust`, `typescript`, `javascript`, `python`, `go`)
- `--limit <LIMIT>`: Most results to show, from 1 to 200
- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook code status`

Report whether the index matches the files on disk

Hashes every file git lists, so it is slower than the quick check that search commands run first.

Example: `playbook code status --json`

- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook code symbol`

Find where a name is declared

Matches the exact qualified name first (a top level symbol's qualified name is its plain name), then the name, then the name ignoring case, then the name as a prefix.

Example: `playbook code symbol PaymentService --kind class`

- `<NAME>`: Name to look up
- `--kind <KIND>`: Only this kind, for example `function`, `class` or `method`
- `--lang <LANG>`: Only files of this language: rust, typescript, javascript, python or go (one of `rust`, `typescript`, `javascript`, `python`, `go`)
- `--path <PATH>`: Only files under this path prefix, for example `lib/payment/`
- `--limit <LIMIT>`: Most results to show, from 1 to 200
- `--json`: Print one JSON document

### `playbook commands`

List every playbook command, what it does and who may run it

Built from this binary's own command tree, so it lists only the commands the binary has. One line per command, with its subcommands. A name ending in `!` or a line marked `(user-only)` is for the user to run; `(read-only)` runs freely. Give a group to list its subcommands with their flags. Reads nothing and writes nothing.

Example: `playbook commands pr`

- `<GROUP>`: Command or group to list, such as `pr` or `worktree review`
- `--json`: Print a JSON array with one object per command: command, purpose, access, args, subcommands, intents

### `playbook commit`

Run the git steps of `/playbook:commit`

Subcommands: `all`, `prepare`, `run`

### `playbook commit all`

Stage everything, commit with a drafted message, and push

Refuses the default branch. Stages with `git add -A`, prints `NO_STAGED_CHANGES` when there is nothing to commit, drafts a conventional message from the staged files with no model unless `-m` is given, then commits, rebases when behind and pushes like `run`. A rejected push is never forced. Exits 1 on any failure.

Example: `playbook commit all`

- `-m, --message <MESSAGE>`: Commit message (default: drafted from the staged files)
- `--auto`: Auto mode: never force a push
- `--no-signoff`: Leave the sign-off trailer off
- `--json`: Print one JSON report that always exits 0, the outcome in `verdict`
- `--args-stdin`: Read the flags and the worktree phrase from stdin; stages per `-A`/`-u`

### `playbook commit prepare`

Stage, format, and print what a commit message is drafted from

Refuses the repo's default branch. Prints `NO_STAGED_CHANGES` when there is nothing to commit, else `BRANCH=`, the changed files and the diff.

Example: `playbook commit prepare -A`

- `-A`: Stage everything first (`git add -A`)
- `-u`: Stage tracked changes first (`git add -u`)
- `-a`: Replace the last commit

### `playbook commit run`

Commit, rebase when behind, and push

Reads the message from stdin, or from `--message-file`. Adds a sign-off per `commit.signOff` and signs when `user.signingkey` is set. A rejected push is never forced. Exits 1 on any failure.

Example: `playbook commit run --message-file /tmp/msg.txt`

- `--message-file <MESSAGE_FILE>`: File with the commit message (default: read stdin)
- `-a`: Replace the last commit
- `--auto`: Auto mode: never force a push
- `--no-signoff`: Leave the sign-off trailer off
- `--no-type-check`: Skip the check that the commit type fits the files. A docs-only change is not `feat`, and a lock-file bump is not `fix`
- `--no-prose-check`: Skip the prose check. It flags a dash, a curly quote, a banned word or a contrast phrase in the message

### `playbook completions`

Print a shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish

Example: `playbook completions zsh`

- `<SHELL>`: Shell to print the script for (one of `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`)

### `playbook config`

Read and change playbook settings in any tier

Settings come from tiers, highest first: repo, org, global, then the built-in default. `get` and `list` show which tier supplied a value.

Example: `playbook config set autoReview.enabled true`

Subcommands: `apply-proposal`, `export`, `get`, `import`, `list`, `set`

### `playbook config apply-proposal`

Apply the settings that `pbsync config pull` proposed

Shows each proposed value next to your current global value and asks before it stores anything. Only keys that may sync are accepted, and each value is checked like `config set`. A project value still wins over the global one. Nothing changes unless you answer yes or pass `--yes`.

Example: `playbook config apply-proposal --yes`

- `--yes`: Apply without asking

### `playbook config export`

Print every stored setting as one JSON document

Settings live in a database, not hand-editable files. Export gives you a readable copy, and `config import` loads one back.

Example: `playbook config export > playbook-config.json`

### `playbook config get`

Show a setting's value and which tier it came from

Example: `playbook config get autoReview.enabled`

- `<KEY>`: Dotted setting name, such as `autoReview.enabled`

### `playbook config import`

Load settings from a JSON document made by `config export`

Every key and value is checked first, and nothing is stored if any is invalid. Use `-` to read standard input.

Example: `playbook config import playbook-config.json`

- `<FILE>`: JSON file to read, or `-` for standard input

### `playbook config list`

List every setting with its value and source tier

### `playbook config set`

Change a setting

Writes to the repo tier unless you pass `--org` or `--global`. The per-user `update.*` keys go to the global tier, and `--org` is refused for them.

Example: `playbook config set autoReview.enabled true`

- `<KEY>`: Dotted setting name, such as `autoReview.enabled`
- `<VALUE>`: New value; it is read as the type the setting expects
- `--org`: Write to the org tier instead of the repo tier
- `--global`: Write to the global tier instead of the repo tier

### `playbook deliver`

Commit, push and open or update a PR from any worktree

Stages per flag, commits when something is staged (message from `--message` or `--message-file`), rebases onto the base, pushes, then opens or updates the PR through `gh`. Refuses the default or a protected branch and a detached HEAD, never skips hooks or signing, and only force-pushes with a lease after its own rebase. Exit codes: 0 delivered, 3 refused, 4 rebase conflict, 5 a git or gh call failed, 6 PR closed or a required check failed, 7 wait timed out, 8 auto-merge did not queue, 9 nothing to do.

Example: `playbook deliver --dir ../wt -A --message "fix(x): y" --title "fix(x): y" --ready`

- `--dir <DIR>`: Worktree to deliver from (default: the current directory)
- `-A`: Stage everything first (`git add -A`)
- `-u`: Stage tracked changes first (`git add -u`)
- `--staged`: Commit only what is already staged (the default)
- `--message <MESSAGE>`: Commit message
- `--message-file <MESSAGE_FILE>`: File with the commit message
- `--title <TITLE>`: PR title
- `--body <BODY>`: PR body
- `--body-file <BODY_FILE>`: File with the PR body
- `--base <BASE>`: Base branch (default: the open PR's base, a parent PR branch, or the default branch)
- `--ready`: Open or mark the PR ready for review
- `--draft`: Open or return the PR as a draft
- `--auto-merge`: Queue auto-merge and verify it queued
- `--wait`: Wait until the PR merges, closes, or a required check fails
- `--timeout <TIMEOUT>`: Seconds to wait with `--wait`
- `--dry-run`: Print the plan and change nothing
- `--ticket <TICKET>`: Ticket key for the branch (`none` turns the ticket rules off)
- `--issue <ISSUE>`: GitHub issue number the PR handles
- `--json`: Print JSON instead of text
- `--branch <BRANCH>`: Refuse unless `--dir` is on this branch
- `--auto`: Auto mode: never force a push; a branch that needs a force is parked

### `playbook deps`

Install the tools a Brewfile lists, keeping any already on PATH

Example: `playbook deps ensure Brewfile`

Subcommands: `ensure`

### `playbook deps ensure`

Install missing Brewfile tools with Homebrew

Leaves each tool already on PATH alone, and reads the `brew` and `tap` lines of the Brewfile.

Example: `playbook deps ensure --builtin`

- `<BREWFILE>`: Brewfile to read, `Brewfile` in the current directory by default
- `--builtin`: Read the Brewfile built into this binary instead of a file

### `playbook doc`

Read a PDF or Office file as text with the bundled converter

Conversion is local, bounded in size, time, memory and output, and never uses OCR or a hosted service. The text is printed as untrusted document content. A long document is printed in slices, and the full text is kept in a private cache for a day.

Example: `playbook doc read report.docx`

Subcommands: `read`, `status`

### `playbook doc read`

Print a document as Markdown, framed as untrusted content

Supports pdf, docx, doc, odt, rtf, epub, pptx, ppt, odp, xlsx, ods and csv. A scanned PDF with no text layer reports that it needs OCR.

Example: `playbook doc read report.pdf --section 2`

- `<FILE>`: Document to read
- `--json`: Print one JSON object instead of the framed text
- `--offset <OFFSET>`: Character offset to start the slice at (default 0)
- `--limit <LIMIT>`: Most characters to print, capped at docs.displayChars
- `--section <SECTION>`: Print one section by its number from the section index

### `playbook doc status`

Say which document converter is in use, or that none was found

### `playbook doctor`

Check the playbook setup, or read one fact the check uses

`playbook doctor` with no subcommand runs `playbook doctor check`, the full health check the `/playbook:doctor` command uses. It only reads. The other subcommands print one fact each, such as pending migrations, plugin version or hook wiring, and help when a layer reports a miss.

`playbook doctor --fix` repairs playbook's own files after an upgrade and prints the list of what still needs you, the same as `playbook migrate`. At a terminal it first asks whether to turn attribution OFF, the default, by adding the missing `attribution` keys; that yes is the only Claude Code setting it writes. A no stores attribution ON.

Example: `playbook doctor`

Example: `playbook doctor pending-migrations`

- `--fix`: Run the safe migrations for playbook's own files, then list what needs you

Subcommands: `check`, `models`, `pending-migrations`

### `playbook doctor check`

Check the seven playbook layers and print a status table

Reads your settings, shell files and PATH, and lists a PASS, INFO, WARN or FAIL row for each layer, then the review config, stale worktrees and pending migration notices. Always exits 0 when it could run the checks.

- `--json`: Print the rows as JSON

### `playbook doctor models`

Show the model tiers, any overrides and the fallback chain in use

Also says whether your own fallback replaces playbook's, and when the effort in force makes the chain start at Haiku.

- `--json`: Print the report as JSON

### `playbook doctor pending-migrations`

List the manual migration findings that need you

Prints one line per finding, or nothing when none is pending.

### `playbook effort`

Set playbook's own ceiling on effort, or inspect one component's

`playbook effort list` shows every command, skill and agent with its shipped effort and effective level. `playbook effort resolve agents reviewer` says which agent file to dispatch under the ceilings. Set a per-component ceiling with `playbook config set --global effort.agents.reviewer medium`. `playbook effort suggest` reads your usage and lists agents where a change looks safe or needed.

`auto` (the default) sets no ceiling, so Claude Code's own `maxEffortLevel` decides how high effort may go. Each skill, command and agent still keeps the effort it ships with. `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max` set playbook's own ceiling. The key is `maxEffortLevel`, named like Claude Code's. The effective ceiling is the lower of this and Claude Code's own `maxEffortLevel`, which playbook only reads and never changes. Sessions started with `playbook cc` or `playbook ccd` get the ceiling. With no level, shows both values and the one that wins.

The ceiling lowers the `effort` an orchestrator passes when it spawns an agent, the default effort the launcher adds and what the binary reports. It does not cap a command or skill that ships its own effort, a level you state for the session, or a spawn that skips the resolve step, because only Claude Code's `maxEffortLevel` setting can, and playbook never writes it.

Example: `playbook effort xhigh`

- `<LEVEL>`: One of auto, low, medium, high, xhigh or max
- `--json`: Print the status as JSON (with no level)

Subcommands: `apply`, `choose`, `list`, `log`, `reset`, `resolve`, `suggest`

### `playbook effort apply`

Apply the proposed effort patch to playbook's config, after approval

Builds the same patch as `suggest --patch`, shows it, and asks `y/N`. `--yes` approves without asking, and is required when not at a terminal. Writes only playbook's own config: the global tier, a backup of the previous `effort.*` keys under `~/.config/playbook/effort/`, a ledger and a change log. Never goes below an agent's quality floor, never touches the reviewer, the auditor or any agent marked costly to miss, and never exceeds a ceiling. Claude Code's settings are not touched.

Example: `playbook effort apply --range 90d`

- `--range <RANGE>`: One of 30d, 60d, 90d, month or all
- `--yes`: Approve without asking

### `playbook effort choose`

Choose an effort for one dispatch from its diff

Does nothing while `effort.auto` is `off` (the default). With `suggest` it logs what it would pick and the dispatch keeps the default. With `on` it names the `effort` to pass to the `Agent` call on the base agent, picked strictly between the agent's quality floor and every ceiling, raised (to `high` at most) for risky or large diffs and lowered only for small clean ones. An agent marked costly to miss is never lowered. Any error gives the default. Every choice is appended to a local log (`playbook effort log`).

Example: `playbook effort choose reviewer --base origin/main --json`

- `<AGENT>`: Agent name, such as `reviewer`
- `--base <BASE>`: Read the diff shape from `git diff --numstat <ref>`
- `--lines <LINES>`: Changed lines, when not using --base
- `--files <FILES>`: Changed files, when not using --base
- `--bytes <BYTES>`: Diff size in bytes
- `--path <PATHS>`: Touched path, repeated for several, when not using --base
- `--lens <LENS>`: Review lens, such as `security`
- `--json`: Print JSON

### `playbook effort list`

List every component with its shipped effort and effective level

- `--json`: Print JSON

### `playbook effort log`

Show the automatic effort choices that were logged

Each row has the time (UTC), component, default and chosen level, the inputs and the reason. The log is local and append only.

Example: `playbook effort log --limit 20`

- `--limit <LIMIT>`: How many of the latest rows to show
- `--json`: Print JSON

### `playbook effort reset`

Undo what `effort apply` changed, in one command

Restores each key the patch changed to its earlier value, unless you edited it since. `--all` also sets every other `effort.*` key in the global tier back to its default. A backup is written first.

Example: `playbook effort reset --all`

- `--all`: Also reset every `effort.*` key to its default

### `playbook effort resolve`

Show one component's shipped effort, ceiling and effective level

For an agent it also names the file to dispatch and every file allowed under the ceiling.

`--cap <level>` adds a ceiling from the calling command, for example `review` holding its reviewer to `medium`. The lowest of the cap and the user's ceilings applies.

Example: `playbook effort resolve agents reviewer --cap medium --json`

- `<KIND>`: One of agents, commands or skills
- `<NAME>`: Component name, such as `reviewer` or `review`
- `--cap <CAP>`: Extra ceiling from the caller: low, medium, high, xhigh or max
- `--json`: Print JSON

### `playbook effort suggest`

List agents where a change to effort looks safe or needed (read only)

Reads the local usage store and the quality floor table and prints, for each agent, its dispatches, reruns and overrides, the cost per effort level, and whether lowering is permitted or something needs a look. Lowering is only ever proposed down to the benchmark floor. Nothing is written: not the store, not memory, not any settings file. Cost is per model and effort bucket, shared with the main session.

Example: `playbook effort suggest --range 90d --json`

- `--range <RANGE>`: One of 30d, 60d, 90d, month or all
- `--json`: Print JSON
- `--patch`: Print a proposed config patch instead (still read only)

### `playbook eval`

Check how well the review triage classifier sorts real PRs

Each case is a PR with a known answer per review lens. Costs one `gh pr diff` fetch and one live `claude` call per case, so run it by hand or on a schedule.

Example: `playbook eval review-triage`

Subcommands: `bench`, `review-triage`

### `playbook eval bench`

Benchmark agent roles across models and effort levels

Each case is a fixed prompt with an objective check (a planted bug found, a claim judged right, a test that passes), so no judge model is involved. It prints pass rate, cost and time per role, model and effort. It estimates the cost first and refuses to start above `--max-cost-usd`, and stops mid run when the spend reaches it. Needs a logged-in `claude`; it makes real API calls.

With `--strategy`, the implementer cases run with tools in a scratch git repo, comparing one dispatch per TDD step against one per Work Unit.

Example: `playbook eval bench --role fact-checker --model haiku,sonnet --effort low,medium --runs 2`

- `--cases <CASES>`: Case file or directory; defaults to the cases shipped in the playbook repo
- `--role <ROLE>`: Only these roles (comma separated)
- `--id <ID>`: Only cases whose id starts with one of these (comma separated)
- `--model <MODEL>`: Models to try (aliases such as haiku, sonnet, opus)
- `--effort <EFFORT>`: Effort levels to try
- `--runs <RUNS>`: Calls per case, model and effort
- `--max-cost-usd <MAX_COST_USD>`: Spend cap in US dollars; the run is refused above it
- `--jobs <JOBS>`: Calls in flight at once
- `--json`: Print JSON instead of a table
- `--list`: List the cases and exit
- `--strategy <STRATEGY>`: Run the `tdd_repo` implementer cases with tools in a scratch git repo. Use one dispatch per TDD step (`per-step`) or one per Work Unit (`per-wu`)

### `playbook eval review-triage`

Run the review triage classifier on each case

Compares each result with the known answer. Needs network access, a logged-in `gh`, and a working `claude` with a live API key. Exits 0 when no lens was wrongly skipped and no case errored, and 1 otherwise. Re-run it whenever the triage prompt changes.

Example: `playbook eval review-triage`

- `<FIXTURES>`: Case file to run; defaults to the cases shipped in the playbook repo
- `--prompt <PROMPT>`: Triage prompt to send; defaults to the one shipped in the playbook repo

### `playbook gate`

Record and check plan verdicts used as gates

Verdicts are stored per worktree, keyed by plan.

Subcommands: `check`, `record`, `snapshot`

### `playbook gate check`

Check that recorded phase verdicts still pass

Exits 0 only if every named phase is PASS or WARN and its source is unchanged. Exits 1 on any other verdict, a stale one, or no phases.

Example: `playbook gate check my-plan plan adversarial test-review`

- `<PLAN_SLUG>`: Plan slug to check
- `<COMMAND>`: Command running this check
- `<PHASES>`: Phase names to check
- `--source <SOURCE>`: File with the current source content, compared against what each verdict saw. Defaults to the shared draft, `<plans>/<slug>.gate-source.md`
- `--json`: Print one JSON object instead of text (exit codes stay the same)

### `playbook gate record`

Save a phase verdict for a plan

Reads a phase agent's output, finds its `VERDICT:` line, and stores it.

Example: `playbook gate record my-plan plan adversarial out.md`

- `<PLAN_SLUG>`: Plan slug the phase belongs to
- `<COMMAND>`: Command that produced this verdict
- `<PHASE>`: Which phase this verdict is for
- `<INPUT>`: File with the phase agent's output, or "-" to read stdin
- `--source <SOURCE>`: File with the source content the verdict covers. Used to spot a stale verdict later. Defaults to the phase's snapshot, `<plans>/<slug>.gate-source.<phase>.md`
- `--stuck`: Store a FAIL report as STUCK. Use it when the revise and re-run loop stopped because the blocking findings made no progress. Refused for any other verdict

### `playbook gate snapshot`

Freeze the plan draft for each gate phase about to run

Copies `<plans>/<slug>.gate-source.md`, the draft as it stands, to `<plans>/<slug>.gate-source.<phase>.md` for every phase named, so each phase records its verdict against what it actually reviewed. Prints the snapshot paths. Fails, copying nothing, when the draft file is missing.

Example: `playbook gate snapshot my-plan adversarial test-review`

- `<PLAN_SLUG>`: Plan slug
- `<PHASES>`: Phase names to snapshot for

### `playbook gc`

Show what playbook state takes space on disk, or clean it up

Lists each store of on-disk state with its size, item count, age and the action a cleanup would take. It changes nothing and takes no lock. With `--yes` it repairs interrupted moves, tombstones items past their limit and deletes tombstones past their grace period. With `--restore` it puts a tombstoned item back where it came from.

Example: `playbook gc`

- `--yes`: Apply the cleanup
- `--restore <ID>`: Restore a tombstoned item by id

### `playbook glossary`

Append entries to the repo's `GLOSSARY.md` file

Subcommands: `add`

### `playbook glossary add`

Append one entry line to `GLOSSARY.md` at the repo root

Example: `playbook glossary add "WU: Work Unit"`

- `<ENTRY>`: Entry text to append

### `playbook handoff`

Save and show notes that carry over to the next session

A handoff is a markdown note for one directory. The next session started there loads it when the SessionStart hook is installed and runs, and `/playbook:handoff-show` loads it on demand.

Subcommands: `check`, `facts`, `save`, `show`, `status`, `template`

### `playbook handoff check`

Check a handoff read from stdin for section shape and dashes

### `playbook handoff facts`

Print the git facts for the "Where we are now" section

- `--dir <DIR>`: Directory to read (default: the current one)

### `playbook handoff save`

Save the handoff note read from stdin for the next session

- `--dir <DIR>`: Directory the handoff belongs to (default: the current one)
- `--session <SESSION>`: Session id the handoff is for. Only the start that follows that session's `/clear` loads it, so parallel sessions never share one

### `playbook handoff show`

Print this directory's handoff without using it up

- `--all`: Print every waiting handoff, not just the newest
- `--dir <DIR>`: Directory to show (default: the current one)

### `playbook handoff status`

Show recent session starts and this directory's handoff counts

### `playbook handoff template`

Print the rules and template for writing a handoff

### `playbook hooks`

List the hooks that `playbook setup` wires into Claude Code

Subcommands: `list`

### `playbook hooks list`

Print every hook with its event, matcher and what it does

Lists the hooks setup adds to settings.json, grouped by purpose. Changes nothing.

### `playbook learn`

Gather the repo facts that `/playbook:learn` reads

Subcommands: `collect`, `preflight`

### `playbook learn collect`

Count the git history or the repo layout

Feeds the `/playbook:learn` collectors. `git` prints contributors, churn hotspots, commit types, remote branch prefixes, recent tags and commits per month. `structure` prints the top level, languages, entry points, build manifests with their scripts and targets, test and lint config, Dockerfiles, CI, infrastructure as code, migrations, model files and `scripts/`. Both print one JSON object, read only through `git`, with every count capped.

Example: `playbook learn collect git structure`

- `<ROLES>`: Which to collect: `git`, `structure`, or both (one of `git`, `structure`)

### `playbook learn preflight`

Name the repo and memory store, probe the tools, and tally JIRA keys

### `playbook manifest`

Check that tracked files sit in allowed top-level paths

Subcommands: `check`

### `playbook manifest check`

Check every tracked file is at an allowed top-level path

Exits 0 when all pass and 1 otherwise.

- `<REPO_ROOT>`: Repo root to check (default: the repo you are in)

### `playbook memory`

Manage the memory graph that sessions read from

Subcommands: `context`, `export`, `import-claude`, `rebuild`, `stats`

### `playbook memory context`

Print the repo's slice of the memory graph as markdown

Shows the facts in scope, typed edges and the anchor index. When there is nothing to show it prints one `Memory context: none (<reason>)` line and exits 0. A missing default graph is rebuilt from the fact files first.

- `--repo <REPO>`: Repo slug (`owner/name`); defaults to the origin remote's slug
- `--graph <GRAPH>`: Graph JSON file; defaults to the graph in `~/.config/playbook/data/memory.db`

### `playbook memory export`

Print the memory graph as JSON

The graph lives in `~/.config/playbook/data/memory.db`, rebuilt from the fact files. This prints the document older versions kept in `memory.graph.json`, for tools that read that shape. A missing database is rebuilt first.

Example: `playbook memory export --json`

- `--json`: Print JSON (the only format)

### `playbook memory import-claude`

Copy notes from Claude Code's auto memory into playbook memory

One way and opt in. It only reads Claude Code's memory for this project (`~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/*.md`) and never changes, moves or deletes anything there. Each note becomes a playbook fact in this repo's project memory. A note already imported (tracked by content hash on the playbook side) and a fact that already exists are skipped, so running it again copies nothing.

Example: `playbook memory import-claude --dry-run`

- `--dry-run`: Show what would be copied and write nothing
- `--from <FROM>`: Read this directory instead of the project's Claude Code memory

### `playbook memory rebuild`

Rebuild the memory graph from every fact on disk

Memory is rebuilt on its own when a fact is saved, so you only need this after editing fact files by hand. The graph is written to `~/.config/playbook/data/memory.db`; the fact files in `~/.config/playbook/memory/` stay the source of truth, so the database is safe to delete. Prints the same summary as `playbook memory stats`.

- `--json`: Print the summary as JSON

### `playbook memory stats`

Summarize the memory graph without changing it

Prints the database path, size and last rebuild time, the fact count per scope (global, org, project), the node count, the edge count per relation, the anchor count, and the dangling edges (target missing) and anchors (path missing on disk). Anchors are checked only for the repo you run it in, when it has an `origin` remote. Read only: a missing database is reported, not built.

Example: `playbook memory stats --json`

- `--json`: Print the summary as JSON

### `playbook migrate`

Bring playbook's own files up to date with this binary

Runs the migrations that write only playbook's own files, then records this binary as the one that ran them. The ones that run once start only after an upgrade, and the checks that repair a file run every time. A migration waits for the release named in its `since`. Nothing runs after a downgrade. It never writes Claude Code settings. It ends with the list of what still needs you, one bullet per item with why it matters and the command that fixes it: `playbook setup` for a change to Claude Code settings or a shell file, and its own fix for a report. The session start then stops repeating a report it printed. A run also updates the playbook plugin through `claude plugin update`, then says to restart Claude Code. A missing `claude` command or a failed update prints the command to run and does not change the exit code. `--no-plugin` or `playbook config set update.plugin off` turns this off. `update`, the install script and `doctor --fix` run the same step.

Exit codes: 0 when it finished or had nothing to do, 1 when the record could not be read or written, a migration failed, or another playbook process held the lock.

Example: `playbook migrate --status`

- `--status`: List each migration with its release, scope and state, writing nothing
- `--dry-run`: Show the migrations a run would start and what needs you, writing nothing
- `--json`: Print JSON for tools
- `--no-plugin`: Leave the playbook plugin in Claude Code as it is. By default a run updates it with `claude plugin update`, unless the config key `update.plugin` is `off`

### `playbook mode`

Choose whether playbook asks questions or decides on its own

`ask` is the default. `auto` lets commands pick the recommended option and keep going. The choice is stored per repo.

Example: `playbook mode auto`

Subcommands: `ask`, `auto`, `status`

### `playbook mode ask`

Turn auto mode off for this repo, so playbook asks again

### `playbook mode auto`

Turn auto mode on for this repo

### `playbook mode status`

Show the current mode and where it came from

- `--json`: Print one JSON object instead of a line of text
- `--flag <FLAG>`: Report as if a command ran with `--auto` or `--ask`, and warn when the hooks would disagree (one of `ask`, `auto`)

### `playbook path`

Print the path of a playbook storage directory

Prints one of this repo's storage directories. For those kinds it first moves any legacy directories from the old repo-local location. `data` and `plugin-root` skip that move. `plugin-root` prints the installed playbook plugin directory instead. It looks at `PLAYBOOK_PLUGIN_DIR`, then the `installPath` Claude Code recorded, then `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT`, then the newest plugin cache directory. When none is usable it prints one line naming each place tried and exits 1. `--create` does not apply to it.

Example: `playbook path plans`

- `<KIND>`: Which directory to print (one of `plans`, `implement`, `worktrees`, `handoff`, `data`, `plugin-root`)
- `--create`: Create the directory when it does not exist

### `playbook plan`

Save plan checkpoints, write Work Unit briefs, clear scratch files

Subcommands: `brief`, `checkpoint`, `cleanup`

### `playbook plan brief`

Write the brief file for each Work Unit

`/playbook:implement` gives these files to its subagents. Each `<OUT>/<wu-id>.brief.md` holds a short header (plan, worktree, scoped verify), the Work Unit's own section of the plan verbatim, and a "Relevant memory" list of the facts anchored to its files or matching its title. With `code.briefFactsTokens` above 0 it adds a `Callers` block of use sites from the code index, cut to that many tokens. Every id is checked first: a missing one writes nothing and exits 1. Prints the paths written, one per line.

Example: `playbook plan brief docs/plan.md WU-1 WU-2 --out /tmp/briefs --verify 'cargo test {tests}'`

- `<PLAN>`: Plan or blueprint file
- `<WUS>`: Work Unit ids, such as `WU-1`
- `--out <OUT>`: Directory to write the briefs into
- `--worktree <WORKTREE>`: One worktree path for every brief
- `--worktree-base <WORKTREE_BASE>`: Directory holding one worktree per Work Unit, named by its lower case id
- `--verify <VERIFY>`: Scoped verify command; `{tests}` and `{files}` become the Work Unit's paths
- `--repo <REPO>`: Repo slug (`owner/name`) for the memory scope; defaults to the origin remote's
- `--graph <GRAPH>`: Graph JSON file; defaults to the graph in `~/.config/playbook/data/memory.db`

### `playbook plan checkpoint`

Print a topic's checkpoint path, or save the checkpoint

Without `--write` it creates the plans directory and prints the path, then `found` or `not-found`. With `--write` it replaces the checkpoint with stdin under a directory lock. A failed save prints a one-line notice and still exits 0, so planning continues without resume safety.

Example: `playbook plan checkpoint my-topic`

- `<SLUG>`: Kebab-case topic slug, or the ticket id in lower case
- `--write`: Replace the checkpoint with stdin

### `playbook plan cleanup`

Remove the scratch files a finished plan leaves in the plans directory

Removes exactly `<slug>.checkpoint.md`, `<slug>.checkpoint.md.lock` and `<slug>.gate-source*.md` from `playbook path plans`, never the final plan or its quality report. Prints the removed file names, one per line. Safe to repeat: nothing to remove exits 0. Exit 1 for a bad slug or flags, 2 when a symlink leaves the directory or a removal fails (nothing removed after a refusal). `--stale` lists leftovers of every slug that already has a final plan and deletes them only with `--yes`.

Example: `playbook plan cleanup my-topic --dry-run`

- `<SLUG>`: Kebab-case topic slug
- `--dry-run`: Only list what would be removed
- `--json`: Print the result as JSON
- `--stale`: Clear leftovers for every slug that already has a final plan; dry run unless `--yes`
- `--older-than <OLDER_THAN>`: Only clear files at least this many days old. Needs `--stale`. By default a plan being re-planned today is left alone, because files under one day old are kept
- `--yes`: With `--stale`, actually delete

### `playbook plans`

List the plans and ADR blueprints `/playbook:implement` can run

Prints `path<TAB>[status]<TAB>title` per file, or `NO_PLANS`.

- `--json`: Print JSON instead of text

### `playbook plugin`

Manage the playbook plugin in Claude Code, apart from the binary

`install` adds the marketplace and the plugin, for a playbook that did not come from Homebrew. `upgrade` refreshes the marketplace and runs `claude plugin update` for each installed playbook plugin id. Neither downloads a binary. Run `playbook upgrade` to update the binary.

Example: `playbook plugin install`

Subcommands: `install`, `upgrade`

### `playbook plugin install`

Install the playbook plugin and its marketplace into Claude Code

For a playbook that did not come from Homebrew, such as one from the install script, a container, a home server platform like Umbrel or a nix profile. Needs `claude` on PATH. Adds the `amplifiedengineer/marketplace` marketplace unless Claude Code lists it already, and leaves one listed under the old `pragmatic-engineer` name as it is. Turns on `autoUpdate` for the marketplace in `~/.claude/settings.json`, and keeps an explicit `false`. Then installs `playbook@amplifiedengineer`. Claude Code updates a plugin with its marketplace, so that one flag also keeps the plugin up to date; there is no per-plugin key.

You asked for it, so `update.plugin` set to `off`, `PLAYBOOK_SKIP_PLUGIN_UPDATE` and a CI environment do not stop it. Prints one line per step. A second run reports every step as done and changes nothing. Exits 1 when `claude` is not on PATH or a step fails.

Restart Claude Code or run /reload-plugins after an install.

Example: `playbook plugin install`

- `--json`: Print one JSON object in the shared envelope, and exit 0 whatever the result

### `playbook plugin upgrade`

Upgrade only the playbook plugin and its marketplace

Refreshes the marketplace, then runs `claude plugin update` for every installed playbook plugin id, `playbook@amplifiedengineer` and the old `playbook@pragmatic-engineer`. You asked for it, so `update.plugin` set to `off`, `PLAYBOOK_SKIP_PLUGIN_UPDATE` and a CI environment do not stop it. Prints one line per plugin. Exits 1 when an upgrade fails, `claude` is not on PATH, or the marketplace refresh failed while the plugin lags; an up to date plugin, one the marketplace has not published yet and a missing plugin exit 0.

Restart Claude Code or run /reload-plugins after an upgrade.

Example: `playbook plugin upgrade`

- `--json`: Print one JSON object in the shared envelope, and exit 0 whatever the result

### `playbook pr`

Prepare and open PRs, and pick a review depth

These are the mechanical steps behind `/playbook:pr-create`.

Example: `playbook pr prepare --base main`

Subcommands: `ci-wait`, `comments`, `create`, `land`, `land-wait`, `merge`, `prepare`, `reply`, `review-triage`, `rules`, `stack`, `status`

### `playbook pr ci-wait`

Wait for a PR's required checks to finish

Prints a `checks total=.. pending=.. fail=.. cancel=..` line per read, then `CI_VERDICT=` one of NONE, FAIL, CANCELLED, PASS or TIMEOUT.

Example: `playbook pr ci-wait 12 --timeout 600`

- `<PR>`: PR number
- `--timeout <TIMEOUT>`: Give up after this many seconds
- `--interval <INTERVAL>`: Seconds between reads
- `--all`: Wait on every check, not only the required ones
- `--settle <SETTLE>`: Wait this many seconds before the first read, so checks register

### `playbook pr comments`

Resolve a PR and fetch its review threads and comments

Takes the command's arguments as one string (`#12 --bots --dry-run -y`). Prints the PR, head SHA, your login and the flags, and writes the threads and issue comments as JSON under `/tmp`.

- `<ARGS>`: Command arguments as one string, such as `#12 --bots`

### `playbook pr create`

Push the branch and open a PR from a drafted title and body

Opens a draft unless the `pr.draft` setting is `false`.

Example: `playbook pr create --title "fix(x): y" --body-file /tmp/body.md`

- `--title <TITLE>`: PR title, at most 72 characters
- `--body-file <BODY_FILE>`: File holding the PR body
- `--base <BASE>`: Base branch for the PR (default: the repo's default branch)
- `--dir <DIR>`: Work in this directory instead of the current one
- `--ticket <TICKET>`: Ticket key for the branch (`none` turns the ticket rules off)
- `--issue <ISSUE>`: GitHub issue number the PR handles

### `playbook pr land`

Wait for checks, arm auto-merge, and wait for the merge

Prints `LAND=<verdict>` and a JSON report. Exit codes: 0 merged, 3 a gate (draft, waiting on a base PR, head moved, review required, changes requested, needs a rebase), 6 a check failed or the PR closed, 7 still waiting (call again with `--settle 0`), 8 auto-merge did not queue. Never uses `--admin` and never deletes the branch.

Example: `playbook pr land 12`

- `<PR>`: PR number
- `--timeout <TIMEOUT>`: Give up after this many seconds in total
- `--interval <INTERVAL>`: Seconds between reads
- `--settle <SETTLE>`: Seconds to wait for the first checks to appear (use 0 on a repeat call)
- `--dir <DIR>`: Work in this directory instead of the current one

### `playbook pr land-wait`

Wait for a PR to merge or hit a gate

Prints a status line per read (state, merge state, review, auto-merge), then `LAND_VERDICT=` one of MERGED, REVIEW_GATE, CHANGES_REQUESTED, RESTATE or TIMEOUT.

Example: `playbook pr land-wait 12`

- `<PR>`: PR number
- `--timeout <TIMEOUT>`: Give up after this many seconds
- `--interval <INTERVAL>`: Seconds between reads

### `playbook pr merge`

Merge a PR with auto-merge, or as an admin squash

Prints `merge_rc=<code>` (or `admin_rc=`) and then what `gh` said. Always exits 0, so the caller reads the code.

Example: `playbook pr merge 12 --admin`

- `<PR>`: PR number
- `--admin`: Squash with admin rights instead of arming auto-merge
- `--match-head <MATCH_HEAD>`: Refuse the merge unless the PR head is this commit

### `playbook pr prepare`

Run pre-flight checks and gather what a PR draft needs

Finds the branch and base, checks the repo is ready, writes the diff to a scratch file, and prints labeled lines for the PR drafter.

Example: `playbook pr prepare --base main`

- `--base <BASE>`: Base branch for the PR (default: the repo's default branch)
- `--ticket <TICKET>`: Ticket id to cite (default: one found in the branch name)
- `--dir <DIR>`: Work in this directory instead of the current one
- `--json`: Print one JSON report instead of labeled lines
- `--args-stdin`: Read the command's flags and the worktree phrase from stdin

### `playbook pr reply`

Post one reply on a PR, from a file

`--thread ID` replies in a review thread (ID is the `databaseId` of the thread's first comment, as `pr comments` writes it); `--issue` comments on the PR itself. The body is read from `--body-file`, so quotes, backticks and newlines need no shell escaping. It refuses an empty body, an em or en dash, and AI attribution. Prints `Posted: <url>` and the body.

Example: `playbook pr reply --pr 12 --thread 345 --body-file /tmp/reply.md`

- `--pr <PR>`: PR number
- `--thread <THREAD>`: Reply in the review thread whose first comment has this `databaseId`
- `--issue`: Comment on the PR itself
- `--body-file <BODY_FILE>`: File holding the reply text
- `--repo <REPO>`: `owner/name`; defaults to the current repo

### `playbook pr review-triage`

Choose a quick or deep self-review for a PR

Asks a small model three times. Anything but a unanimous `quick` becomes `deep`.

Example: `playbook pr review-triage --pr 12`

- `--pr <PR>`: PR number (default: the current branch against its base)
- `--base <BASE>`: Base branch when no PR number is given (default: the repo's default branch)
- `--dir <DIR>`: Work in this directory instead of the current one

### `playbook pr rules`

Cut the skill rules a PR title and body need

Reads the writing-style and engineering-standards skills from the plugin root (`playbook path plugin-root` prints it), writes four files under `/tmp`, checks each, and prints their paths. A failed check prints `ERROR: ...` and exits 1. With `--commit` it writes only the commit-message slice of writing-style. When the plugin lacks one of the files, the copies built into this binary are used and stderr says so.

- `--plugin-root <PLUGIN_ROOT>`: Plugin root (default: `playbook path plugin-root`, else the built-in copies)
- `--commit`: Write only the slice a commit message needs

### `playbook pr stack`

Find the PRs stacked with a PR

Reads the GitHub stack API, then falls back to the branch chain. Takes the arguments as one string (`#12 --json --max-prs 6 --max-lines 3000`). Prints a summary, or JSON with `--json`. `--context` writes one shared review context under `/tmp/pr-stack-<pr>`. `--digest` prints what the open PRs above the PR change, per file. `map --stack <file> --findings <file>` gives each finding to the PR whose diff holds the line and lists the findings a PR above changes under `fixed_above`.

- `<ARGS>`: Command arguments as one string, such as `#12 --json`

### `playbook pr status`

Read what the finish flow needs to know about a PR, in one call

One call for the finish flow. With `--json` it prints the shared envelope (`ok`, `code`, `meaning`, `error`) around the report and exits 0 even on failure: read `ok` and `code`. A usage error still exits 2. Without `--json` it prints the same report as text and exits with the code.

Example: `playbook pr status 12 --json`

- `<PR>`: PR number
- `--json`: Print the JSON envelope and exit 0
- `--flag <FLAG>`: Treat the run mode as this one, as `mode status --flag` does (one of `ask`, `auto`)
- `--dir <DIR>`: Work in this directory instead of the current one

### `playbook prose`

Check prose against the writing-style rules

Subcommands: `check`

### `playbook prose check`

Lint files for banned phrases, structures and em or en dashes

Prints `path:line: finding` for each problem. Fenced code, inline code, URLs, file paths and quoted lines are skipped. Exits 0 unless `--strict` is given and a hard finding exists, or a file cannot be read. With `GITHUB_ACTIONS=true` it prints annotations.

Example: `playbook prose check README.md`

- `<FILES>`: Files to check
- `--strict`: Exit 1 when a hard finding exists

### `playbook review`

Run the mechanical steps behind the review commands

Subcommands: `checks`, `prepare`, `size`, `suggest`, `triage-merge`

### `playbook review checks`

Run a project's own type check, lint and tests in a directory

Prints their output. A failing check is output, not an error.

Example: `playbook review checks /tmp/review-wt`

- `<DIR>`: Review worktree to run in

### `playbook review prepare`

Resolve the PR, report-only or posting, and in-place or worktree

Takes the raw arguments of the review command as one string. Prints `KEY=value` lines: PR, REPO, PR_NUMBER, HEAD_SHA, AUTHOR, SELF_REVIEW, SELF_MODE, MODE, WT and REVIEW_JSON. On a problem it prints `error: ...` and exits 1.

Example: `playbook review prepare deep "#4265 --self"`

- `<KIND>`: Which review: `quick` or `deep` (one of `quick`, `deep`)
- `<ARGS>`: Review command arguments as one string, such as `#12 --self`
- `--auto`: Accepted for compatibility; auto mode does not skip the post question

### `playbook review size`

Measure a diff and say which review path it takes

Counts the changed lines of `BASE...HEAD` and prints `lines=N files=M path=single|swarm`. A diff of at most 150 changed lines takes the `single` path, one reviewer holding every lens; a larger one, or any run with `--all-lenses`, takes `swarm`.

Example: `playbook review size --base main`

- `--base <BASE>`: Ref the diff starts from
- `--head <HEAD>`: Ref the diff ends at
- `--all-lenses`: Always take the swarm path
- `--dir <DIR>`: Repo directory to measure in. Defaults to the current directory

### `playbook review suggest`

Recommend a quick or a deep review from the diff

Reads the changed files from git (the branch against the default branch, no network) or from `gh` when a PR number is given, and applies a fixed rule list: size, files, packages touched, risky paths (auth, crypto, secrets, CI, release, hooks, guards, migrations, dependencies, the command surface, plugin commands, skills and agents over the small cut), a security label, the test ratio, and changes that cannot alter behavior (docs, lock files, renames, tests). Prints `recommendation=quick|deep`, `confidence=high|low`, up to four `reason:` lines, a `signals:` line, a `scope=` line and, with `--scope stack`, a `stack:` line. Low confidence means no rule was decisive; the answer then leans quick for your own change (a local branch always is) and deep otherwise. Docs and lock file lines do not count toward size, and files outside crates, packages, apps, services, libs and plugins count together as one `root` package. The cuts are the `review.suggest.*` config keys.

`--scope stack` measures every open PR in the PR's stack together: merged PRs are left out, closed PRs are skipped, and a PR outside a stack is measured alone. A stack with more open PRs than `review.stackMaxPrs` is answered deep without reading their files.

Example: `playbook review suggest 4265 --json`

- `<PR>`: PR number (default: the current branch against the default branch)
- `--scope <SCOPE>`: What to measure: this PR alone, or every open PR in its stack (one of `this-pr`, `stack`)
- `--base <BASE>`: Base branch when no PR number is given. Defaults to the repo's default branch; pass the parent branch for a stacked change
- `--dir <DIR>`: Work in this directory instead of the current one
- `--json`: Print JSON instead of text lines

### `playbook review triage-merge`

Complete a review-triage tier map so no lens is left unclassified

Reads the triage reply (a JSON object of `{lens: {tier, reason}}`) from `--tiers FILE`, or `-` for stdin, and prints the full map as JSON plus a `Triage: lens=tier, ...` line. A missing or unusable reply, a lens the reply left out, and a tier other than `skip`, `cheap-check` or `full-lens` all become `full-lens`.

Example: `playbook review triage-merge --lenses security,logic --tiers triage.json`

- `--lenses <LENSES>`: Every lens that was sent to triage, comma separated
- `--tiers <TIERS>`: File holding the triage reply, or `-` for stdin; omit when triage returned nothing
- `--force <FORCED>`: Fix a lens's tier whatever triage said, as `lens=tier:reason` (repeatable)

### `playbook route`

Say which model, effort and agent a kind of task goes to

One routing table for every command that dispatches agents. Kinds: mechanical, classify, check, review, write, implement, design. Only `implement` reads `--tier` (low, medium or high). The answer includes whether the user must approve first (the top model, the high tier, or a task that failed twice). `routing.escalate` decides what happens then: `ask` tells you to ask the user, `auto` (default) proceeds (auto mode and `auto.budgetUsd` still cap the spend), `deny` returns the cheaper route. Your effort ceiling always wins.

Example: `playbook route implement --tier medium --json`

- `<KIND>`: One of mechanical, classify, check, review, write, implement or design
- `--tier <TIER>`: One of low, medium or high. Only `implement` reads it
- `--failures <FAILURES>`: How many times this task already failed
- `--json`: Print the decision as JSON

### `playbook run-context`

Read the run mode and effort ceiling

Gives a command's Step 0 the mode and the ceiling in one call. Reads `--auto` and `--ask` from the command's arguments (exit 2 when both are present), and prints one JSON object: `mode`, `source`, `hook_mode`, `warning`, and `ceiling` when `--command` names the command. `ceiling` is the highest effort the user allows, or null.

Example: `playbook run-context --command implement --args "--auto"`

- `--command <COMMAND>`: Command name, such as `implement`. Adds the effort ceiling
- `--args <ARGS>`: Raw arguments of the command, as one string

### `playbook sanitize`

Remove AI attribution lines from message text

For callers that are not an agent hook, such as a git `commit-msg` hook or CI. Each subcommand rewrites FILE in place unless `--check` is given, and prints one line per removed line to stderr: its number and the shape of the attribution, never its text. Without `--check` the exit code is always 0, even when FILE cannot be read or written.

Subcommands: `commit-msg`, `pr-text`

### `playbook sanitize commit-msg`

Clean a commit message file, such as git's `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG`

Example: `playbook sanitize commit-msg .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG`

- `<FILE>`: File holding the message
- `--check`: Report what would be removed, without writing. Exits 1 if anything would be removed, and 2 if FILE cannot be read

### `playbook sanitize pr-text`

Clean a PR title or body saved to a file

Example: `playbook sanitize pr-text /tmp/body.md`

- `<FILE>`: File holding the text
- `--check`: Report what would be removed, without writing. Exits 1 if anything would be removed, and 2 if FILE cannot be read

### `playbook segment`

Run the git recipes `/playbook:implement` uses for a Segment

Subcommands: `branch`, `size`

### `playbook segment branch`

Put HEAD on the branch a Segment is built on

Names the branch `<type>/<plan-slug>-s<N>-<title>` and creates it from the right base: the default branch for independent Segments, the previous Segment's branch for stacked ones (fetched when it is not local), and always the fetched `origin/<default>` under `--land`. The single topology creates nothing and reports the current branch and tip. Prints `branch=<name> base=<sha> base_ref=<ref>`. Exits 1 when the branch already exists.

Example: `playbook segment branch --type feat --plan-slug my-plan --n 2 --title "Parser core" --topology stacked --prev-branch feat/my-plan-s1-schema`

- `--type <KIND>`: Conventional commit type for the branch name, such as feat
- `--plan-slug <PLAN_SLUG>`: Plan slug
- `--n <N>`: Segment number
- `--title <TITLE>`: Segment title, kebab-cased and truncated into the branch name
- `--default-branch <DEFAULT_BRANCH>`: Default branch of the repo
- `--dir <DIR>`: Repo directory to run in. Defaults to the current directory
- `--topology <TOPOLOGY>`: How the plan's Segments are delivered (one of `stacked`, `independent`, `single`)
- `--prev-branch <PREV_BRANCH>`: Previous Segment's branch, for a stacked Segment past the first
- `--land`: Branch off the fetched origin default branch, at the land boundary

### `playbook segment size`

Measure a Segment against its base

Prints `lines=N files=M` for `BASE...HEAD`.

Example: `playbook segment size --base main`

- `--base <BASE>`: Base ref of the Segment
- `--dir <DIR>`: Repo directory to run in. Defaults to the current directory

### `playbook sessions`

List recent agent sessions and their state

Shows the repo, branch, worktree, linked PR, state, context size and cost of each session. Read only. A session is done when the PR of its branch is merged or closed, and stale after `sessions.staleAfterDays` without activity. Suggestions are printed, never acted on, and a worktree with uncommitted changes is flagged, never removed.

Example: `playbook sessions --json`

- `--json`: Print the sessions as JSON

Subcommands: `list`, `sweep`

### `playbook sessions list`

List recent sessions (the default)

- `--json`: Print the sessions as JSON

### `playbook sessions sweep`

Show what a sweep would close for each finished session

Judges each finished session's worktree with the same guards as `playbook worktree remove`: landed, clean, unlocked and not in use. A stale session is listed but not swept. Only the dry run exists: it removes nothing, stops no process and closes no tab or pane.

Example: `playbook sessions sweep --dry-run`

- `--dry-run`: Report only and change nothing (required)

### `playbook settings`

Create or check the shared settings template

Subcommands: `check`, `gen`

### `playbook settings check`

Check the shared settings template is valid

Exits 0 when valid and 1 with a message when not.

Example: `playbook settings check seed/shared-settings.json .`

- `<TEMPLATE>`: Shared settings template to check
- `<REPO_ROOT>`: Repo root that every hook command must resolve inside

### `playbook settings gen`

Create the shared settings template from a live settings.json

Takes the hooks and status line from the live file and keeps the permissions of the current seed. Prints the new seed.

Example: `playbook settings gen ~/.claude/settings.json seed/shared-settings.json`

- `<SRC>`: Live settings.json to start from
- `<SEED>`: Current seed, whose permissions block is kept

### `playbook setup`

Install or repair your local Claude Code setup

Safe to run again: it only touches what is missing or out of date. In a terminal it asks about each optional part (hooks, status line, PATH, the system prompt, the `pb` short name) unless you answer with a flag. Each part has `--x` and `--no-x`. With `--yes`, unanswered parts use their defaults, and every asked part is on: hooks, the status line, PATH, the system prompt and `pb`. The system prompt stays off when `systemPrompt.enabled` is false or an earlier install had none, and `pb` stays off after a stored no. Telemetry is on by default too: the question defaults to yes and `--yes` is a yes, but `--yes` alone never replaces an off switch you set. Without a terminal and without `--yes`, only PATH is on: hooks, the status line, the system prompt, `pb` and telemetry stay off unless you pass their flag. `--only telemetry` (or a bare `--telemetry`) runs just that part; `--only` takes any parts and leaves everything else alone.

The security defaults (permissions rules) are never asked about and stay off unless you pass `--security` or set `security.defaults` to true. Without them, `setup` leaves any permissions you already have untouched.

Before it asks anything, setup prints a plan of each part and the files it edits. `--dry-run` shows what would change on your machine and changes nothing. `--explain` describes a part, or every part, and changes nothing.

Example: `playbook setup --no-hooks --system-prompt`

- `--plugin`: Install or update the playbook plugin in Claude Code with the `claude` command. Given by name it runs even without a terminal, with `update.plugin` off or in CI
- `--no-plugin`: Leave the playbook plugin as it is
- `--hooks`: Wire every playbook hook into settings.json (guards, session and worktree hooks)
- `--no-hooks`: Add no playbook hook entries, including the guards in the shared settings
- `--statusline`: Use the playbook status line (sets statusLine.command to `playbook statusline`)
- `--no-statusline`: Do not set or change statusLine in settings.json
- `--security`: Also apply the security defaults (permissions rules). Off unless asked or `security.defaults` is true
- `--no-security`: Do not apply the security defaults, even when `security.defaults` is true
- `--path`: Put the playbook binary on PATH for every shell start
- `--no-path`: Do not edit shell files for PATH
- `--system-prompt`: Install the playbook system prompt (an existing copy is refreshed either way)
- `--no-system-prompt`: Do not install the system prompt. It stores `systemPrompt.enabled` false so `pb cc` starts with Claude Code's own
- `--telemetry`: Answer yes to the telemetry question. Writes the OpenTelemetry variables for the local usage collector into settings.json. Given alone it means `--only telemetry`
- `--no-telemetry`: Do not write telemetry variables into settings.json
- `--short-name`: Add `pb` as a short name for `playbook`. Makes a `pb -> playbook` symlink in the install directory, only when `pb` is free
- `--no-short-name`: Do not add the `pb` short name
- `--completions`: Install tab completion for `playbook` and `pb` in the shell named by `$SHELL`
- `--no-completions`: Do not install shell completion
- `--policy-guard`: Turn the policy guard on (`hooks.policyGuard.enabled`). It denies skipped git hooks, a hand-run gh pr create, Claude Code memory writes and settings.json edits
- `--no-policy-guard`: Do not turn the policy guard on; it is off by default and a stored choice is not changed
- `--attribution`: Attribution ON: Claude Code adds its Co-Authored-By trailer, generated-by line and session link. Removes each `attribution` key in settings.json that holds exactly the off value playbook writes, and stores `attribution.enabled` true
- `--no-attribution`: Attribution OFF. Claude Code adds no trailer, generated-by line or session link. Sets `attribution` in settings.json, replacing your own values. Setup applies this when you choose nothing and have not chosen ON before
- `--codex-hooks`: Register the playbook Bash guards in the hooks.json of Codex (off unless asked)
- `--no-codex-hooks`: Do not register guards in Codex
- `--only <PART>`: Run only these parts and ask nothing. Parts, comma separated: plugin, hooks, statusline, security, path, system-prompt, telemetry, short-name, completions, policy-guard, attribution, codex-hooks. Everything else stays untouched. `playbook setup --only telemetry` turns telemetry on, and `--only attribution` applies attribution OFF unless you chose ON
- `-y, --yes`: Never ask: use the default for every part you did not answer with a flag
- `--dry-run`: Print what would change for each part and change nothing
- `--explain <PART>`: Describe a part, or every part when none is named, and change nothing

### `playbook skills`

Share the playbook skills with other agents

`sync` copies the plugin's skills and commands into the folder that Codex reads, `~/.agents/skills`, as `playbook-*` folders. It never touches folders you made yourself or edited.

Example: `playbook skills sync --dry-run`

Subcommands: `sync`

### `playbook skills sync`

Copy the playbook skills into another agent's skill directory

Without `--agent`, every agent found on this machine is synced. A second run with nothing new changes nothing.

Example: `playbook skills sync --agent codex`

- `--agent <AGENT>`: Sync only this agent (one of `codex`)
- `--dry-run`: Show what would change and write nothing
- `--json`: Print the report lines as a JSON array

### `playbook state`

Inspect playbook's own bookkeeping (migration record, sweep markers)

`list` prints the rows of the `state` table in `config.db`, sorted by key, optionally only those under a prefix. Read only: use `playbook setup` to repair and `playbook config export` to back up the config.

Example: `playbook state list migrations/`

Subcommands: `list`

### `playbook state list`

Print the state rows, sorted by key

- `<PREFIX>`: Only keys that start with this prefix
- `--json`: Print the rows as one JSON object

### `playbook statusline`

Print the Claude Code status line

Claude Code runs this to draw the line at the bottom of a session.

### `playbook tools`

List the commands a session can use for each task

Subcommands: `map`

### `playbook tools map`

Print the map from each task to the command that does it. The session start hook injects this text, so skills can ask for a task by name

- `--json`: Print `[{"intent", "command"}]` as JSON
- `--check`: Exit 1 when the map costs more than its token budget

### `playbook trust`

Mark a directory as trusted in Claude Code

Writes to `~/.claude.json` so Claude Code's first-launch trust prompt does not block `playbook cc` or `playbook ccd`. Always exits 0, even on failure, so a script can call it without checking.

Example: `playbook trust /Users/me/project`

- `<PATH>`: Absolute path of the directory to trust

### `playbook uninstall`

Remove what playbook installed from this machine

Takes out the hook entries and status line that `playbook setup` wrote into `settings.json`, the launcher block in your shell rc files, and the files playbook placed under `~/.config/playbook`. It stops and removes a collector service that an older setup installed, under the current or the 0.37.0 launchd label. Everything else in `settings.json` and the rc files stays, each changed file is backed up first, and memory, sessions and history are never touched. The `playbook` binary stays unless you pass `--remove-binary`. It changes nothing without `--yes`; `--dry-run` lists what would go.

Example: `playbook uninstall --dry-run`

- `--yes`: Go ahead and remove (without it, nothing is changed)
- `--dry-run`: List what would be removed and change nothing
- `--remove-binary`: Also remove the `playbook` binary, its backups and the PATH line the installer added

### `playbook upgrade`

Upgrade playbook to a published release, and its plugin with it

Looks up the latest release and compares it with this binary. When it is newer, shows both versions and asks you to confirm in a terminal; `--yes` skips the question. With no terminal and no `--yes`, it prints the hint and changes nothing. After you confirm, it downloads the release, checks its SHA256 sum and, when `gh` is installed, its build attestation, then swaps the binary and keeps the old one as a backup. In auto mode it refuses unless you pass `--yes`.

Then it runs the plugin step of `playbook plugin install` and `playbook plugin upgrade` so the plugin matches the new binary: it adds the marketplace when it is missing, turns on `autoUpdate` for it, and installs or updates the plugin. Pass `--no-plugin` or set `update.plugin` to `off` to skip that step. To change only the plugin, run `playbook plugin upgrade`.

A Homebrew install is never replaced: `upgrade` checks for a newer release, says Homebrew owns the binary, and tells you to run `brew upgrade playbook`. It exits 0.

`--check` and `--list` change nothing. `--check` exits 0 whether or not a newer release exists, and 1 on an error such as an unreachable release list or an unknown version. `--json` prints one object in the shared envelope and exits 0 whatever the result.

Example: `playbook upgrade --check`

- `--check`: Only report whether an update is available
- `--list`: List published releases
- `--pre`: Consider pre-releases when picking the latest
- `--yes`: Skip the confirmation question, and confirm the upgrade when auto mode is on
- `--json`: Print one JSON object in the shared envelope, and exit 0 whatever the result
- `--no-plugin`: Leave the playbook plugin in Claude Code as it is. By default `upgrade` installs or updates it, unless the config key `update.plugin` is `off`

### `playbook usage`

Show token and cost usage across your sessions

With no subcommand, opens the terminal view, which opens on this week compared with last week. When stdout is not a terminal, or with `--summary`, prints a text summary of estimated cost instead. `--json` prints the same numbers as JSON for scripts. Times and days use your local time zone, shown in the output; `--utc` switches to UTC, or set `usage.timeZone` or `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ` to `local` or `utc`. Ranges: today, week, last-week, month, last-month, 30d, 60d, 90d, all. Weeks start on Monday unless `usage.weekStart` says otherwise. For today, week and month, `--json` adds a comparison with the previous period over the same elapsed span, and `--summary` prints it. The cost per agent and skill, tool latency and health views come from Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export when it is available, see `playbook usage collect`.

Example: `playbook usage --range today`

- `--json`: Print the totals, groupings and live view as JSON
- `--summary`: Print the text summary and exit (every recorded session unless `--range` is given)
- `--range <RANGE>`: Date range, counted in days of the chosen time zone. One of today, week, last-week, month, last-month, 30d, 60d, 90d or all. Default week for the terminal view, 30d for `--json`, all for `--summary`
- `--account <KEY_OR_NAME>`: Show only one account, by key or name. Scopes `--summary` and `--json`, and the terminal view opens on it
- `--utc`: Show times and group days in UTC. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`
- `--local`: Show times and group days in your local time zone. This is the default. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`

Subcommands: `account`, `collect`, `doctor`, `machine`, `prune`, `status`, `stop`

### `playbook usage account`

List the accounts in the usage store, name them and move events

Every usage event carries an account key: the email Claude Code was signed in to, or a `token:` fingerprint. These commands show the keys, give each one a display name and relabel events recorded under the wrong account.

Example: `playbook usage account list`

- `--db <FILE>`: Usage database file to use instead of the default, such as a backup copy
- `--utc`: Show times and group days in UTC. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`
- `--local`: Show times and group days in your local time zone. This is the default. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`

Subcommands: `assign`, `fingerprint`, `list`, `name`, `reconcile`, `sessions`, `undo`

### `playbook usage account assign`

Move events to another account, by time range or by session

Prints how many events and how much cost would move and changes no events until you add `--confirm`. Times are read on your local clock; add `--utc` for UTC. By time, give `--from` and `--to` (the end is not included) and each event moves by its own time. By session, give `--before-session` or `--through-session` with `--from` or `--from-session` as the start, and every event of each session that starts in that span moves. An applied move is numbered and `account undo` reverses it. Running the same move again moves nothing.

To change one session only, add `--session`: it limits the move to the events of that session. With `--from` or `--to` it moves that part of the session; without them it moves the whole session.

Example: `playbook usage account assign --from 2026-11-01T00:00 --to 2026-11-02T12:00 --as personal`

- `--from <FROM>`: First instant to move, like 2026-11-01T00:00 (a bare date means midnight)
- `--to <TO>`: First instant not to move, like 2026-11-02T12:00
- `--from-session <SESSION>`: Start with the sessions from this one on (its id from `account sessions`)
- `--before-session <SESSION>`: End before this session starts
- `--through-session <SESSION>`: End with this session included
- `--session <SESSION>`: Move only events of this session (its id from `account sessions`)
- `--as <KEY_OR_NAME>`: Account key or name that receives the events
- `--was <KEY_OR_NAME>`: Move only events now labeled with this account key or name
- `--confirm`: Apply the move; without it nothing changes
- `--db <FILE>`: Usage database file to use instead of the default, such as a backup copy
- `--utc`: Show times and group days in UTC. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`
- `--local`: Show times and group days in your local time zone. This is the default. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`

### `playbook usage account fingerprint`

Print the account key for CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in this shell

A session started with that variable set is recorded under a key like `token:ab12cd34`, made from the token with a one way hash. This prints the key and never the token. Run it in a shell that has the variable set, then use the key with `account name` and `account assign`.

Example: `playbook usage account fingerprint`

- `--db <FILE>`: Usage database file to use instead of the default, such as a backup copy
- `--utc`: Show times and group days in UTC. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`
- `--local`: Show times and group days in your local time zone. This is the default. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`

### `playbook usage account list`

List the accounts with their events, cost and time span

- `--db <FILE>`: Usage database file to use instead of the default, such as a backup copy
- `--utc`: Show times and group days in UTC. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`
- `--local`: Show times and group days in your local time zone. This is the default. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`

### `playbook usage account name`

Give an account key a display name, or clear it with an empty name

Example: `playbook usage account name you@example.com Company`

- `<KEY>`: Account key shown by `account list`
- `<NAME>`: Display name to show; empty clears it
- `--db <FILE>`: Usage database file to use instead of the default, such as a backup copy
- `--utc`: Show times and group days in UTC. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`
- `--local`: Show times and group days in your local time zone. This is the default. Overrides `usage.timeZone` and `PLAYBOOK_TELEMETRY_TZ`

### `playbook usage account reconcile`

Compare cost on each side of session boundaries with a dashboard

Give the daily totals you read from the Claude web dashboard of the account that owns the later sessions, as `YYYY-MM-DD=amount`. For each session that starts in the window, taken as the boundary, it prints the local cost per listed day before it and from it on, and how far the later side is from the dashboard. The closest boundaries print first. Days are on your local clock; add `--utc` for UTC.

Example: `playbook usage account reconcile --from 2026-10-30 --to 2026-11-04 --dashboard 2026-11-03=285.03`

- `--from <FROM>`: Start of the window, like 2026-10-30
- `--to <TO>`: End of the window (not included)
- `--dashboard <DAY=AMOUNT>`: Dashboard daily total, like 2026-11-03=285.03; repeat for more days
- `--top <TOP>`: Print this many results, closest boundary first; 0 prints all
- `--db <FILE>`: Usage database file to use instead of the default, such as a backup copy
